questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a screening colonoscopy after a positive faecal immunochemical test. He has no abdominal pain, bloating or change in bowel habit. The colonoscopy shows multiple small outpouchings in the sigmoid colon with no inflammation, and a single small polyp is removed from the transverse colon. His abdomen is soft and non-tender.
questions.q: Which term best describes the sigmoid colon findings?
questions.e: Diverticulosis is the presence of diverticula without symptoms. Diverticular disease needs symptoms and diverticulitis needs inflammation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which term best describes the sigmoid colon findings? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: no abdominal pain, bloating or change in bowel habit
multiple small outpouchings in the sigmoid colon
steps.x: Outpouchings (diverticula) in the **sigmoid colon** of a man **over 60** with **no symptoms** and **no inflammation**.

elim: Requires symptoms such as pain, bloating or bowel habit change; he has none.
Requires inflammation or infection; the mucosa is not inflamed and he is well.
A functional symptom diagnosis; it does not produce visible outpouchings.
A twisted sigmoid loop causing obstruction, not small outpouchings.

steps.x: **C. Diverticulosis.** Diverticula with no symptoms = diverticulosis; add symptoms = diverticular disease; add inflammation = diverticulitis.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has a 5 month history of intermittent cramping left iliac fossa pain, bloating and alternating constipation and loose stools. She eats little fruit or vegetables. Her temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 76 bpm. She is mildly tender in the left iliac fossa without guarding. A CT colonography 1 year ago showed sigmoid diverticula.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diverticular disease means diverticula causing symptoms such as LIF pain, bloating and bowel habit change. Without fever or raised markers this is not diverticulitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: intermittent cramping left iliac fossa pain, bloating
steps.x: Known **sigmoid diverticula** now causing **symptoms** (LIF pain, bloating, bowel habit change) but **no fever**.

elim: Possible at her age, but she had imaging showing diverticula only and has no weight loss or bleeding; the picture fits symptomatic diverticula.
Would give acute pain with fever and raised inflammatory markers; she is afebrile with months of intermittent symptoms.
Means diverticula without symptoms; she has pain, bloating and bowel habit change.
Causes bloody diarrhoea and urgency, not intermittent cramps with alternating bowel habit in a low-fibre eater.

steps.x: **B. Diverticular disease.** Symptomatic diverticula without signs of infection = diverticular disease.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has a 2 day history of constant pain in the left lower abdomen and loss of appetite. He has been constipated for years. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. He is tender in the left iliac fossa with no guarding or rebound. Investigations:

visual.title: Where the pain is
visual.caption: Left iliac fossa pain and tenderness: the sigmoid colon, the commonest site of diverticula.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute LIF pain and tenderness with fever, anorexia and raised WCC and CRP is diverticulitis. Appendicitis is the right-sided equivalent in younger patients.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: constant pain in the left lower abdomen
tender in the left iliac fossa
steps.x: Older, chronically constipated man with **acute LIF pain**, **fever**, **anorexia** and raised **WCC and CRP**.

elim: Typically right iliac fossa pain in a younger patient.
Causes gradual bowel habit change, bleeding and weight loss rather than 2 days of fever and tenderness.
Usually a younger patient with chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and often right iliac fossa disease.
Causes massive distension and absolute constipation, not localised tenderness with fever.

steps.x: **D. Diverticulitis.** Acute LIF pain + fever + raised WCC/CRP in an older patient = diverticulitis (the 'left-sided appendicitis').

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman with known sigmoid diverticula has 2 days of left iliac fossa pain that became suddenly much worse 6 hours ago. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. Her abdomen is rigid with guarding and rebound tenderness, worst on the left. An erect chest X-ray is taken (see item resources).

visual.title: Erect chest X-ray
visual.caption: Free air under the diaphragm: a perforated viscus.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Perforated diverticulitis gives LIF tenderness with signs of peritonitis and a systemically unwell patient; the chest X-ray shows free air under the diaphragm.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: left iliac fossa pain that became suddenly much worse
rigid with guarding and rebound tenderness
steps.x: LIF pain in **known diverticular disease**, then sudden worsening with **peritonitis** (rigidity, guarding, rebound), sepsis and **free air**.

elim: Pain out of proportion to signs, usually with AF; it does not start as days of LIF pain with known diverticula.
Also gives free air, but starts with sudden epigastric pain, not 2 days of LIF pain in known diverticular disease.
Causes back pain, shock and a pulsatile mass; it does not cause free intraperitoneal air.
Gives massive distension and obstruction; free air only after late perforation.

steps.x: **B. Perforated diverticulitis.** Localised LIF tenderness progressing to peritonitis and free air = perforated diverticulitis.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has been taking oral antibiotics at home for 4 days for diverticulitis. His left iliac fossa pain is worse and he has had evening fevers and rigors. His temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 108 bpm. A tender, fixed mass is palpable in the left iliac fossa. His CRP has risen from 96 to 210 mg/L.
questions.q: Which complication has most likely developed?
questions.e: A localised perforation walls off as an abscess: swinging fever, worsening pain and a palpable mass despite antibiotics. Free perforation gives generalised peritonitis instead.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which complication has most likely developed? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: worse and he has had evening fevers and rigors
tender, fixed mass is palpable in the left iliac fossa
steps.x: Failure to improve on antibiotics, **swinging fevers**, a **palpable tender mass** and **rising CRP**.

elim: Free perforation would cause generalised rigidity and guarding, not a localised mass.
Antibiotic-associated profuse diarrhoea, not a fixed LIF mass.
Causes pneumaturia, faecaluria and recurrent UTIs, not a tender mass with swinging fever.
A late fibrotic narrowing causing large bowel obstruction, not fever with a tender mass.

steps.x: **D. Diverticular abscess.** Worsening pain, sepsis and a palpable mass on treatment = abscess from a localised perforation.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has had four admissions with diverticulitis over 3 years. He now has 2 weeks of worsening constipation, colicky lower abdominal pain and distension, and has vomited twice today. He has not lost weight. CT shows a long segment of narrowed, thickened sigmoid colon with diverticula and a dilated proximal colon. There is no mass or lymphadenopathy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his bowel obstruction?
questions.e: Repeated episodes of diverticulitis cause fibrosis and a diverticular stricture, which can cause large bowel obstruction. Colonoscopy and biopsy are still needed later to exclude cancer.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his bowel obstruction? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: long segment of narrowed, thickened sigmoid colon
steps.x: **Recurrent diverticulitis**, then large bowel obstruction from a **narrowed, thickened sigmoid** with **no mass**.

elim: Adhesions cause small bowel obstruction after surgery, not a narrowed sigmoid with a dilated colon.
Dilated colon with no mechanical narrowing; CT here shows a fixed narrowed segment.
The commonest cause of large bowel obstruction, but CT shows no mass or nodes and he has recurrent diverticulitis without weight loss.
Causes acute massive distension with a 'coffee bean' loop, not a fixed narrowed segment.

steps.x: **D. Diverticular stricture.** Recurrent inflammation leads to fibrosis and stricture, which causes large bowel obstruction.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man is told after a CT scan that he has many diverticula in his sigmoid colon. He has a BMI of 33, works at a desk all day and rarely exercises. He eats mostly white bread and processed food and has opened his bowels with straining every 3 to 4 days for many years.
questions.q: Which is the most likely key driver of his diverticula?
questions.e: Chronic constipation with a low-fibre diet raises intraluminal pressure and straining, which pushes mucosa out through weak points. Obesity and a sedentary lifestyle add risk.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely key driver of his diverticula? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: straining every 3 to 4 days for many years
mostly white bread and processed food
steps.x: Years of **straining** and infrequent stools on a **low-fibre diet**, with obesity and a sedentary life.

elim: Causes malabsorption and villous atrophy, not colonic outpouchings.
Protective; a low-fibre diet is the risk factor.
Causes bloating and diarrhoea after dairy, not diverticula.
Not a cause of colonic diverticula.

steps.x: **A. Chronic constipation.** Chronic constipation (with low fibre) raises intraluminal pressure and is the key driver of diverticula.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman with known diverticular disease has had left iliac fossa pain for 3 days. This morning the pain spread across her whole abdomen. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 98/62 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. She is lying very still and is in pain when the trolley is knocked.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
questions.e: Perforated diverticulitis causes peritonitis: the patient is systemically unwell with rigidity, guarding and rebound tenderness, and lies still because movement hurts.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: pain spread across her whole abdomen
in pain when the trolley is knocked
steps.x: Known diverticular disease, pain that has **spread across the abdomen**, sepsis, lying still and pain on jolting: **peritonitis**.

elim: Periumbilical bruising seen in severe pancreatitis, not perforated diverticulitis.
Right upper quadrant catch on inspiration in cholecystitis.
Suggests an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Right iliac fossa pain on pressing the left side, seen in appendicitis.

steps.x: **A. Board-like rigidity with rebound tenderness.** Perforated diverticulitis: systemically unwell with rigidity, guarding and rebound tenderness.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man has 3 days of left iliac fossa pain and fever. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 94/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. He is confused. There is a tender, poorly defined mass in the left iliac fossa with localised guarding. His white cell count is 21 × 10⁹/L and CRP 286 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sepsis, peritonism and a palpable mass mean complicated diverticulitis (abscess, perforation, fistula or obstruction). It is managed as a surgical emergency.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: tender, poorly defined mass in the left iliac fossa
steps.x: LIF pain with **sepsis** (hypotension, confusion), **peritonism** and a **palpable mass**.

elim: Symptoms from diverticula without infection; he is septic with a mass.
Asymptomatic diverticula only.
A functional disorder that never causes fever, sepsis or a mass.
Localised tenderness and fever in a well patient; sepsis and a palpable mass mean complications.

steps.x: **A. Complicated diverticulitis.** LIF pain + fever + peritonism + mass + sepsis = complicated diverticulitis, a surgical emergency.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has known sigmoid diverticula. For a year she has had episodes of left iliac fossa cramps and bloating that settle with laxatives. She now has 2 days of more constant left iliac fossa pain and her doctor is deciding whether she has developed diverticulitis.
questions.q: Which feature would most strongly support diverticulitis rather than diverticular disease?
o: Fever with a raised white cell count
questions.e: Diverticulitis is inflammation or infection of diverticula, shown by fever and raised WCC and CRP. Pain, bloating, bowel habit change and tenderness occur in diverticular disease too.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which feature would most strongly support diverticulitis rather than diverticular disease? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: episodes of left iliac fossa cramps and bloating
more constant left iliac fossa pain
steps.x: She already has **diverticular disease**; the question is what marks **inflammation or infection** of the diverticula.

elim: Common in symptomatic diverticular disease without infection.
A typical feature of diverticular disease.
Present in both diverticular disease and diverticulitis.
Occurs in both; it does not show inflammation.

steps.x: **C. Fever with a raised white cell count.** Diverticulitis = inflammation/infection: fever, raised WCC and CRP, loss of appetite.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man comes to the emergency department with 2 days of left iliac fossa pain and a temperature of 38.0°C. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. He is tender in the left iliac fossa without guarding. He is passing urine normally and is eating a little.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: First-line tests are FBC, CRP and U&Es to show inflammation and dehydration or AKI. CT confirms the diagnosis; colonoscopy is avoided acutely.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: 2 days of left iliac fossa pain
tender in the left iliac fossa without guarding
steps.x: Suspected **acute diverticulitis** in a stable patient; you need to see the inflammatory response and kidney function first.

elim: Adds little in suspected diverticulitis without obstruction.
Avoided in acute diverticulitis because of the risk of perforation.
Used to screen for inflammatory bowel disease in younger patients with chronic diarrhoea.
Not used for acute diverticulitis.

steps.x: **D. FBC, CRP and U&Es.** First-line in diverticulitis: bloods (FBC, CRP, U&Es); CT confirms; colonoscopy later.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has left iliac fossa pain, fever and a tender mass. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 108/70 mmHg. She has guarding in the left iliac fossa. Investigations show a white cell count of 18.4 × 10⁹/L and CRP 240 mg/L. The surgical team suspects complicated diverticulitis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
questions.e: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast is the gold standard; it shows wall thickening, abscess and perforation. Endoscopy is avoided acutely.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: guarding in the left iliac fossa
steps.x: Suspected **complicated diverticulitis** with a mass: you need to see the colon wall, abscess and any perforation.

elim: Limited by bowel gas and less able to show perforation or abscess.
Can show free air but will not show an abscess or the colon itself.
Endoscopy risks perforating inflamed bowel in acute diverticulitis.
Slower and less available; not the standard test.

steps.x: **B. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast.** Gold standard for diverticulitis and its complications: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has 3 days of left iliac fossa pain and fever. His temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. He is tender with localised guarding in the left iliac fossa. His CRP is 164 mg/L. A contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis is performed to confirm the suspected diagnosis of diverticulitis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the CT scan?
o: Dilated caecum with a twisted mesentery
Featureless colon with loss of haustra
Thickened sigmoid colon wall with pericolic fat stranding
questions.e: CT in diverticulitis shows a thickened sigmoid colon wall with pericolic fat stranding. Diverticula are commonest in the sigmoid colon.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on the CT scan? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: left iliac fossa pain and fever
localised guarding in the left iliac fossa
steps.x: Diverticulitis affects the **sigmoid colon**, under the LIF; CT shows the inflamed bowel and surrounding fat.

elim: Suggests caecal volvulus.
The finding in appendicitis, in the right iliac fossa.
Suggests chronic ulcerative colitis ('lead pipe').
A late sign of bowel ischaemia.

steps.x: **E. Thickened sigmoid colon wall with pericolic fat stranding.** CT in diverticulitis: thickened sigmoid wall and pericolic fat stranding.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman is admitted with CT-confirmed acute sigmoid diverticulitis. Her temperature is 38.1°C and pulse rate 92 bpm. She has never had a colonoscopy. Her daughter asks why the team will not look inside her bowel with a camera now to rule out cancer.
questions.q: Which is the main reason colonoscopy is not performed during this admission?
o: Bowel preparation would cause dangerous diarrhoea
Colonoscopy cannot reach the sigmoid colon
High risk of perforating the inflamed bowel
The sedation would worsen her sepsis
questions.e: Colonoscopy is avoided in acute diverticulitis because of the high risk of perforating the inflamed bowel. It is done once inflammation has settled to exclude malignancy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the main reason colonoscopy is not performed during this admission? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: why the team will not look inside her bowel with a camera now
steps.x: The bowel is **acutely inflamed** and its wall is weakened by micro-perforation.

elim: Not the main reason; the danger is to the inflamed bowel wall.
Colonoscopy examines the whole colon including the sigmoid.
CT does not reliably exclude malignancy; that is why colonoscopy is done later.
Not the reason it is avoided.

steps.x: **D. High risk of perforating the inflamed bowel.** Colonoscopy is avoided in acute diverticulitis because of the high risk of perforation; it is done once inflammation settles.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man had CT-confirmed sigmoid diverticulitis 7 weeks ago, treated with oral antibiotics. His pain has settled and he feels well. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. His haemoglobin is 132 g/L. He has never had any examination of the inside of his colon and asks what happens next.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Once acute inflammation has settled, colonoscopy is done to exclude malignancy or an alternative diagnosis. It is avoided during the acute episode.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: never had any examination of the inside of his colon
steps.x: The **acute inflammation has settled** and his colon has **never been inspected**.

elim: Shows obstruction or perforation; it cannot exclude a colonic tumour.
Largely replaced; it cannot take biopsies.
Used for the small bowel; it cannot biopsy and is not used to assess the colon after diverticulitis.
Malignancy must still be excluded once the acute episode has settled.

steps.x: **D. Colonoscopy.** After diverticulitis settles, colonoscopy excludes malignancy or other pathology.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with diverticular disease has had four urinary tract infections in 6 months. He describes air passing at the end of his urine stream and his urine sometimes looks cloudy and brown. Urine culture grows mixed coliforms. CT shows sigmoid diverticula with gas in the bladder. The urologist plans to confirm the fistula.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Pneumaturia, faecaluria and recurrent UTIs with diverticular disease suggest a colovesical fistula. It is diagnosed by cystoscopy or cystography and needs surgical repair.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: air passing at the end of his urine stream
steps.x: **Pneumaturia**, **faecaluria** and **recurrent UTIs** in diverticular disease: a **colovesical fistula**.

elim: Images the kidneys and ureters, not a connection between colon and bladder.
A blood test for prostate disease; it does not show a fistula.
Will not reliably show a colovesical fistula.
Looks for urothelial cancer cells.

steps.x: **A. Cystoscopy.** Colovesical fistula: confirmed by cystoscopy (or cystography), then surgical repair.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has 8 months of intermittent left lower abdominal cramps and bloating, with hard stools every few days. Colonoscopy showed sigmoid diverticula only. He is afebrile, his abdomen is soft and his CRP is normal. He eats very little fruit or vegetables and drinks little water.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Increase dietary fibre and fluid intake
questions.e: Diverticular disease is managed with more dietary fibre, hydration, treating constipation and lifestyle advice. Antibiotics are only for diverticulitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Symptomatic diverticula with **constipation**, a **low-fibre diet** and **no infection**: diverticular disease.

elim: Surgery is not offered for uncomplicated symptomatic diverticular disease.
Lowers fibre, which worsens constipation, the driver of diverticular disease.
For diverticulitis when antibiotics are indicated; he has no infection.
Opioids worsen constipation.

steps.x: **B. Increase dietary fibre and fluid intake.** Diverticular disease: more fibre (fruit and vegetables), hydration, manage constipation, lifestyle advice.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has 2 days of left iliac fossa pain and a temperature of 38.1°C. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 130/84 mmHg. She is tender in the left iliac fossa without guarding. Her CRP is 88 mg/L. She is eating and drinking and the GP decides she can be treated at home with antibiotics. She has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Co-amoxiclav covers the Gram-negative and anaerobic gut flora in diverticulitis. She also needs analgesia, fluids and safety-netting advice.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: left iliac fossa pain and a temperature of 38.1°C
steps.x: **Uncomplicated diverticulitis** in a well patient who needs antibiotics; gut flora are Gram-negative and anaerobic.

elim: Lacks reliable cover against beta-lactamase-producing Gram-negatives and anaerobes.
Mainly for urinary and skin infections; poor anaerobic cover.
Covers atypical respiratory organisms, not gut anaerobes.
Only reaches useful levels in urine; for lower UTI.

steps.x: **D. Co-amoxiclav.** Uncomplicated diverticulitis: analgesia, fluids, co-amoxiclav if indicated, and safety-netting.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man has generalised peritonitis. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 84/50 mmHg despite 2 L of IV fluid. He is on IV antibiotics. CT shows free gas and faeculent fluid throughout the peritoneal cavity from a perforation of the sigmoid colon, which contains many diverticula.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Free perforation with faecal peritonitis needs surgery: Hartmann's procedure resects the sigmoid and forms an end colostomy. Percutaneous drainage is for a contained abscess.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate definitive management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Free perforation** of the sigmoid with **faeculent peritonitis** and septic shock.

elim: For a contained abscess, not free faeculent peritonitis.
For appendicitis; the perforation is in the sigmoid colon.
Far too little for a septic patient with faecal peritonitis.
Removes the right colon; the disease is in the sigmoid.

steps.x: **B. Hartmann's procedure.** Severe diverticulitis needing surgery: Hartmann's procedure (sigmoid resection with end colostomy).

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman admitted with diverticulitis has had IV antibiotics for 3 days but still has swinging fevers. Her temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. She is tender in the left iliac fossa but has no generalised peritonitis. A CT shows a 6 cm rim-enhancing collection next to the sigmoid colon.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: A diverticular abscess that is not settling on antibiotics is managed with CT-guided percutaneous drainage. Hartmann's procedure is kept for free perforation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **contained abscess** on CT, not responding to IV antibiotics, without generalised peritonitis.

elim: Adds nothing; the CT has already shown the abscess.
Avoided in acute diverticulitis; it risks perforation.
She has not settled after 3 days; an abscess this size needs draining.
For free perforation or failure of other measures, not a contained abscess.

steps.x: **D. CT-guided percutaneous drainage.** Diverticular abscess: CT-guided percutaneous drainage with antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman has 2 days of left iliac fossa pain, vomiting and fever. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 114 bpm, BP 100/64 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. She has localised guarding in the left iliac fossa. Her CRP is 230 mg/L and creatinine 148 µmol/L (baseline 80).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Admit for IV antibiotics, IV fluids and surgical review
Discharge with oral co-amoxiclav and safety-netting
questions.e: An unwell patient with diverticulitis is admitted for IV antibiotics, IV fluids and surgical review. Home oral co-amoxiclav is for well patients only.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Diverticulitis with **sepsis**, **vomiting** and **AKI**: she cannot be managed at home.

elim: Avoided acutely because of perforation risk.
Suitable only for a well patient with uncomplicated diverticulitis.
For diverticular disease, not acute infection.
Surgery is for perforation or failure to respond; she needs resuscitation and review first.

steps.x: **A. Admit for IV antibiotics, IV fluids and surgical review.** Severe or unwell diverticulitis: admit, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, surgical review.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man has a diverticular stricture of the sigmoid colon after many episodes of diverticulitis. He now has 3 days of absolute constipation, colicky pain, distension and vomiting. His caecum is 11 cm on CT and is tender. Colonoscopic biopsies 2 months ago showed fibrosis without malignancy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Recurrent inflammation and fibrosis cause a diverticular stricture and large bowel obstruction, which is treated by laparotomy. A dilated tender caecum warns of impending perforation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Large bowel obstruction from a **fibrotic diverticular stricture** with a **dilated, tender caecum**.

elim: For an abscess, not a fibrotic stricture.
Will not open a fixed fibrotic stricture in an obstructed patient.
Treats infection; the problem is a mechanical stricture.
Malignancy has been excluded; he needs the obstruction relieved.

steps.x: **C. Laparotomy.** Diverticular stricture causing obstruction: laparotomy (resection).

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has a barium enema that shows many diverticula, almost all in the sigmoid colon. A medical student asks why diverticula form at particular points in the bowel wall and why the sigmoid colon is affected most.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Absent muscularis propria throughout the sigmoid colon
Herniation where vasa recta penetrate the muscularis propria under high pressure
Mucosal ulceration that heals with outpouching
Neoplastic proliferation of the colonic mucosa
questions.e: Diverticula form at weak points where the vasa recta penetrate the muscularis propria. The sigmoid colon has the highest intraluminal pressures, so it is affected most.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: almost all in the sigmoid colon
why diverticula form at particular points
steps.x: The question wants **where** (weak points in the wall) and **why sigmoid** (pressure).

elim: The muscle layer is present; the weak points are only where vessels pass through.
This describes inflammatory pseudopolyps, not diverticula.
Produces polyps and tumours, not outpouchings.
The process in Crohn's disease.

steps.x: **B. Herniation where vasa recta penetrate the muscularis propria under high pressure.** Diverticula form where vasa recta penetrate the muscularis propria; the sigmoid has the highest intraluminal pressure.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with sigmoid diverticulosis asks why his lifelong constipation matters. He eats very little fibre and strains to pass small hard stools. His GP explains how this has led to the outpouchings in his colon.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Bacterial invasion of the colonic wall
Raised intraluminal pressure causing herniation of mucosa and submucosa
Reduced colonic blood flow from atherosclerosis
Thinning of the colonic mucosa from laxative use
questions.e: Chronic constipation and a low-fibre diet raise intraluminal pressure and straining, causing herniation of mucosa and submucosa through weak points in the wall.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: strains to pass small hard stools
steps.x: **Low fibre** and **straining** mean small hard stools and a colon that has to squeeze hard.

elim: This is how diverticulitis develops, not how diverticula form.
The mechanism of ischaemic colitis.
Not the mechanism of diverticula.
Not a cause of diverticula.

Viral infection of the colonic mucosa

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with recurrent diverticulitis has noticed bubbles passing with his urine and, on two occasions, brown particles in it. o: Bladder outflow obstruction from an enlarged prostate
Erosion of an inflamed diverticulum into the bladder
Gas-forming organisms in a stone in the kidney
Reflux of urine up the ureters
Transitional cell carcinoma invading the colon
questions.e: An inflamed diverticulum stuck to the bladder can erode into it, forming a colovesical fistula. Gas and faeces then pass into the urine and cause recurrent UTIs.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of his urinary symptoms? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

steps.x: **Pneumaturia** and **faecaluria** with a thickened sigmoid stuck to the bladder: a **colovesical fistula**.
